hints.content:
###Getting started

**Key idea:** Parallel lines have the same slope.

###Step 1: Find the slope

Slope of the given line:

>$\blueD{\dfrac{1}{2}}$

Slope of the parallel line:

>$\purpleC{\dfrac{1}{2}}$



[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: A coordinate plane. Two lines slant up from left to right. Both move up one units and to the right two units.

hints.content:
###Step 2: Substitute the known point into linear equation

The parallel line will have a slope of $\purpleC{\dfrac{1}{2}}$ and pass through the point $\redD{(9,-6)}$.  Let's start from the point-slope form of the equation of the parallel line, then solve for $y$.  [[☃ explanation 1]]

>$\begin{align}
y-\redD{(-6)} &= \purpleC{\dfrac{1}{2}}(x-\redD{9})\\\\\\
y+6 &= \purpleC{\dfrac{1}{2}}x -\dfrac{9}{2} \\\\\\
y &= \purpleC{\dfrac{1}{2}}x \greenD{-\dfrac{21}{2}}
\end{align}$

options.explanation:
The **point-slope form** of a linear equation is a rearrangement of the slope formula.

>$\begin{align}
m &= \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \\\\\\
m(x_2 - x_1) &= y_2 - y_1 \\\\\\
m(x - x_1) &= y - y_1 &&\text{Generalize.}\\\\\\
\end{align}$

This equation is true for any point $(x, y)$ on a given line, where $(x_1,y_1)$ is also a point on the line.

hints.content:
###Answer

The equation of the parallel line is $y = \purpleC{\dfrac{1}{2}}x \greenD{-\dfrac{21}{2}}$.



[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: A coordinate plane. The x- and y-axes both scale by one. Two lines slant up from left to right. The first line is at negative four at the y axis and moves up one unit and to the right two units. The second line has a point at nine, negative six and moves up one unit and to the right two units.

question.content:
**Write the equation of a line that is *parallel* to ${y=\dfrac{1}{2}x-4}$ and that passes through the point ${(9,-6)}$.**
